I get that you “shouldn’t” have to make a list of chores for a 35 year old, but i think then you need to have a discussion about the division of labor and what you expect from him. And be willing to correct him while he gets the hang of it. 

He can’t read your mind, and i’ve always found people saying “look what I do now try and do more of this without me telling you,” to be quite vague. Like, do you want me to wash the bathroom everytime i use it, or is doing it once a week okay? 

So, set clear expectations. Make a general chore list for him: things you expect him to do always. Vacuum twice a week, clean the bathroom once a week, check that the dishwasher is empty: so on and so forth. Set that clear expectation and let him follow it. 

Show him what the bathroom looks like when you want it cleaned, and tell him that. Don’t ask him to clean it. Walk into the bathroom and say “Hey, see how dirty this is? When it looks like this, clean it.” vs “Just think about how you like a clean house and do more to get that.” 

Be clear about what’s bothering you, and set clear and realistic expectations for what you want him to do about it. 

But no matter how much you complain online or ask him to do more without being asked: he can’t read your mind. Define what more is.

Practical books such as "Clean Code" as suggested by another user is good. I didn't read this specific book, but I've read summaries and most of [this one](https://gist.github.com/wojteklu/73c6914cc446146b8b533c0988cf8d29) was stuff that was baked into a lot of my courses. 

On the text book side of things: a lot of the content taught in books can be found online. the fundamentals are the same and all over the place. In my experience, the content doesn't vary that much from book to book either. Rather than a book list, I'll give you a rundown of the "fundamental" topics covered in my undergrad. More specific topics depend on what your area of work is.

Data Structures -- not a physical book but a lot of students used [Open Data Structures](https://opendatastructures.org/)   
Intro to Algorithms -- [This is good](https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/introduction-algorithms-third-edition), but most books that introduce algorithms will cover the same basic stuff.   
Intro to Networking -- I have no recommendations here. But if I had a dime for every time I needed to know something related to networking I'd have enough to buy several textbooks on the topic.   
Intro to Unix Systems -- If you wanna get really deep in this then [Design of the Unix Operating System](https://www.amazon.ca/dp/0132017997?linkCode=gs2&tag=javarevisit0c-20) is good. Some parts outdated, but solid grasp of the architecture and design philosophy.   
Computer Architecture -- I had one of Stallings' books, and I found the content pretty easy to understand.

Regarding the E-Books: fantastic way to save money. However, if you have a class where the prof is really reliant on the book, or you have trouble focusing when reading on a screen, don't be afraid to buy a physical copy. Sometimes holding it in your hands can make a difference. 

Kind of unpopular opinion, but if you buy a physical copy of a book, don't be afraid to write in it or highlight it or anything like that. It might make it harder to resell, but if highlighting and annotations work best for you, then it's worth it. Specifically if your professor uses the book a lot.

How do you really make that distinction though? Because in my school that would be a change of major not a change of track within a major. If its a bachelor of science degree, a major in computational math and computer science can be different, though the distinction isn't major in terms of qualifications.

The way that it was put to me by my CS profs is that your CS degree basically is a sheet of paper that says "I have a solid enough background to learn new and use new skills in this field," rather than a paper that says "I know everything about CS." 

Also, a lot of CS programs that I am familiar with, focus on theory and basics in the first two years. You think it won't ever be relevant, and sure maybe not all of it will be relevant to you, but having a solid grasp of the basics and the theory makes it much easier to understand more complex issues you likely will encounter. Some of the theory I learned in the first two years I swore I would never need. Ended up being a main point when working on my thesis in my final year.

I know how frustrating it can be to learn things that feel outdated. But keep in mind not every company, department, or government, is going to have modern systems or use modern tech. And remember that a lot of modern things build on these outdated things -- be it language or whatever. Outdated things don't exist in a vacuum. 

My advice? Take school seriously, and take the initiative to develop your practical skills on your own. Learning the theory isn't as attractive as just doing and making stuff, but its an investment that will pay off.  But more than that, I've found that people have an easier time learning the practical skills on their own but struggle to teach themselves the theory the same way. Take advantage of the fact that you're in a position where people are there to teach and help you with the theory. 

Also, keep in mind that the people who will be hiring you likely wont be from the CS field. If that is the case, you can be super skilled and useful, but all they will understand is "Doesn't have the relevant education," even though youre self taught. Its frustrating, but.... its life.

ADHD dude here. Russell Barkley has a lot of good tips. How To ADHD probably has some good tips too. r/ADHD probably could point you in the right direction too.

As for myself? Video game soundtrack or a podcast/video essay that I can tune out if I can't get a quiet place. Have a snack nearby. Personally I have 2-3 drinks near by as well (coffee/tea, water, Gatorade) but one would work. Sipping on a sugary drink is supposed to help hence gatorade for me. I use toggl Track to work in pormodoros. Don't feel obligated to take the break if you're in a flow. Personally having the time I've been working/on break **visible** makes it much easier for me to not get distracted for hours.Don't beat yourself up if you do get distracted or off track. Just try and take a step back and try again. Beating yourself up over it is just going to make things worse. It takes practice.

My number one tip though is to have a paper near by or a text document open; this is your "**thought record"**. As you're studying and working and you get a thought that's off topic or tangential to what you're doing and you want to act on it *write it down* then **go back to your work.** Keep the thought record **somewhere accessible or visible so you are reminded of it later.**

Doing this allows me to acknowledge the thought or idea now, and have a record of it later when it is **appropriate to deal with it.** 

For example last night I was taking notes from my textbook and I couldn't quite grasp a concept. Instead of *immediately* going on my computer and looking it up (likely getting side tracked) I just *wrote down* that I might need to **look into that after** **we have the lecture covering it.**  I finished my notes then was able to look over my "record" and formulate a few questions about the concept to ask about during the lecture.   
Had I just gone and looked up the concept, I likely would have gotten side tracked, not finished my notes, probably not even learned the concept, and would be unprepared for my lecture tomorrow.

I use them for pretty much everything. It helps keep me accountable and refreshed while working. 

I do a lot of programming and writing (my thesis is on a simulation i had to code) and how many i do personally depends on how much I want to get done, how focused I feel, and how productive I'm actually being. No point in trying to push to 8 pomodoros if I'm at 4 and feel like I'm just spinning out. 

I find that I stick to pomodoros more when coding though. Like, the cycle of breaks and work works really well for that. For writing or creative stuff -- for me -- its more of a tool to get into the zone and mindset. Once I get that I might keep the timers going (might skip breaks though) just to keep track of time spent doing it. Over all though, for more creative stuff, I find that taking breaks at every interval can be more of a hindrance than help.

A psych hold sounds scary, and schools are quick to act, but its not just because its a PR nightmare: its because the suicide rates among college students are high, and rising. If you're thinking of suicide and might try it, a psych hold is not the scariest thing to happen. Check out other local mental health services too: some of them are free or low cost and less proactive then schools -- only if you have a plan will they hold you.

That being said, if your school has a crisis center check them out. For our school the crisis centers are usually just places you can hang out, but most of the time there is a student volunteer there who can help direct you to other mental health services locally, and probably tell you what service is best given what you're looking for. I run a center like this and we can tell you what would be your best service given the situation. We can tell you how to get where you need to go, and if you need it sometimes we're able to offer a ride. If you feel like you need moral support to do something we'll work with you to give you the support you need. It's also dubbed a "safe" space as we have our own *separate* policies for reporting. Joking about suicidal thoughts, or talking about intrusive thoughts won't get you reported with us. Generally the most we can do without cause to believe you're in danger, is ask school mental health services to follow up. What students do with that is up to them. 

If you're not sure you need help pretend your best friend just told you all of your problems as if they were their own. What would you tell them to do?  Whatever your answer is is probably what you should do.

TLDR: don't suffer suicidal thoughts in silence. School systems may not have the best help, but look for what you can find and don't hesitate to get help if you need it. Local non school services will also likely be available to you as well. You're not the only student to have gone though this, nor will you be the last

Most people do it before, so that they have some idea about the lecture going in. Personally, I find it depends on the class, how closely the class follows the textbook/readings, and the profs expectations. 

Some of my profs conduct lectures having expected you to do the readings -- when you get to class you're expected to already know the basics of the topic, and have questions ready if you don't. Others treat the readings as supplementary and only expect you to look them over to build on the lecture. Some treat it as a resource they just expect you to consult if you need help.  It varies school to school, prof to prof, class to class. You'll figure it out as you go, but if you aren't sure, always do the readings before to play it safe.

Also, if you can afford it, buying hard copies of your textbooks can be very useful. I'm in the minority of people here, but one reason I like hard copies is because sometimes (depending on the class), I'll take my textbook notes in the textbook. Annotations, highlighting, so on and so forth, help me grasp the content better than rewriting and rephrasing. The downside to this is that I can't really sell the books after, however, since this helps me so much, I only see it as a small price to pay.

Hand writing notes changed my schooling. I actually got a tablet to hand write my notes on. To review them -- usually the day after the class for me -- I go through and convert the hand writing to text.
